clue.text: City meeting place of Blake and Parry

definitions.meaning: the holy city of the Middle East

definitions.text: meeting place of Blake and Parry
definitions.meaning: William Blake wrote the poem and Hubert Parry set it to music as the famous hymn, so the two men meet in it

explanation.surface: A trivia question about where a poet and a composer once met up.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's poem 'And did those feet in ancient time' was set by Parry as a hymn known by the city's name, sung at English sporting and civic events.
explanation.definitionFit: The hymn shares its title with the ancient holy city, so one name covers both the place and the poem-plus-tune.

definitions.meaning: the American abolitionist who led the raid on Harpers Ferry against slavery

explanation.surface: A palace attendant who opposes slavery.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous men share the name: Victoria's ghillie and the anti-slavery militant.

definitions.meaning: the ordinary upright printing typeface, as opposed to italic
belonging to Rome, the Eternal City

explanation.surface: A respectable kind of city.
explanation.definitionFit: The plain upright font contrasts with italic, and the adjective also means belonging to Rome.

indicators.note: fixed and put back together differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking whose boy mended the winter boots.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket-like frame strapped to the boot for walking over snow is cold-season gear for the feet.

clue.text: Story about gardens is in the same vein

indicators.note: placed around, so the story wraps the other pieces

parts.note: a lie is a story, an untruth
Kew Gardens are the Royal Botanic Gardens in London

explanation.surface: A tale about some gardens told in a similar manner.
explanation.walkthrough: LIE goes about KEW plus IS. KEW is the famous botanic gardens in south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means similarly, in the same way.

indicators.note: placed around, so the witticism goes round the French article

parts.note: a mot is a witty remark, from bon mot
les is French for 'the' (plural)

explanation.surface: A joke at the expense of the French by someone called Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name but is the verb; 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to harass or pester, the same as to pester someone persistently.

clue.text: Drink deeply and very noisily as at first

indicators.note: these words say the piece for 'as' comes before the musical marking

parts.note: qua is a Latin-derived word meaning 'in the capacity of', i.e. as
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Someone gulping a drink loudly, just as they did at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' places QUA ahead of FF; 'and' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To gulp a drink heartily and in large draughts is exactly this verb's sense.

definitions.meaning: a fruit tree related to the pear
Peter, the carpenter who stages the play of Pyramus and Thisbe in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: A tree described as producing Shakespeare plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit tree shares its name with Peter, director of the mechanicals' play in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

indicators.note: something odd is out of the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Butter spread out in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' looks like the dairy product but means flattery, as in buttering someone up. The fodder is LAID OUT AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter is slang for lavish flattery, and fulsome praise is just that.

parts.note: in biology a sport is an organism showing an abnormal variation, i.e. something odd thrown up by nature

explanation.surface: Sport presented as the natural thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A biological sport is a mutant, an abnormal specimen of nature.

clue.text: Meat to scoff in bed, mainly

parts.note: ham is cured pork, a meat
to mock is to scoff or jeer

explanation.surface: Someone eating meat in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoff' looks like eating, matching 'Meat', but here it means jeer. 'mainly' is a pun on the main, the sea: the bed is a sailor's swinging one.
explanation.definitionFit: A slung canvas bed was the sleeping place of sailors on the high seas, so it is a bed of the main.

clue.text: Garland; yes, one is free at this

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers
sure is an informal yes

explanation.surface: A garland offered with a happy assent, as if free for the taking.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'at' this means having free time with no duties pressing.

definitions.meaning: 2 down is ROMAN, and the Latin word a Roman used for good is the same word

explanation.surface: Something is extra good for two people.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' is a cross-reference to 2 down, whose answer leads to the Latin for good.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonus is an extra sum on top of pay, and in Latin the same word was the adjective for good.

parts.note: wise means learned, knowledgeable
crack means first-rate or expert, as in a crack shot

explanation.surface: A scholarly specialist skilled at witty comebacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A quip or smart retort is the stuff of witty banter.

clue.text: Building you once sited la the river

indicators.note: placed within, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in England, a crossword favourite
thou is the old, archaic form of you

explanation.surface: An archaic address to someone who built by a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A shed or privy standing apart from the main house is a small building.

clue.text: To gain time, increase speed first

indicators.note: says the piece for speed goes before the increase

parts.note: tempo is speed of music or activity
a rise is an increase

explanation.surface: Advice to accelerate early to win some time.
explanation.definitionFit: To stall or delay a decision so as to buy time is this verb's sense.

definitions.meaning: informal for a fast pace, as in going along at a fair clip
to defeat or thrash an opponent

explanation.surface: The pace needed to win a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Going 'at a fair lick' means fast, and licking an opponent means thrashing them.

clue.text: Went to bed without rising and got carried away

definitions.text: Went to bed without rising and got carried away

parts.words: Went to bed without rising and got carried away
parts.note: read as someone young who dozed off, never woke, and was taken off by force

explanation.surface: Someone who fell asleep, stayed in bed, and became overexcited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got carried away' looks like losing self-control but means abducted; a young one (a kid) who napped was spirited away.
explanation.definitionFit: Being abducted means literally being carried away by force.

parts.note: Churchill's phrase was a euphemism for a lie, but read literally it means using words wrongly

explanation.surface: A pompous circumlocution for the consequence of a lie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terminological inexactitude' was Churchill's famous euphemism for a lie; here it is taken literally as choosing the wrong term.
explanation.definitionFit: Applying the wrong name or term to something produces a wrongly used label.

parts.note: whist is an old call for silence, like hush

indicators.note: without an end, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: less means without

explanation.surface: Endless pipes playing while silence is demanded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interminable' removes the final S of LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple tin flutes are small pipes.

definitions.note: a gold-rush town in the far north-western US state

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the answer to the other clue referred to by number

explanation.surface: Something located both in a numbered clue and in an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 refers to 17 down, MISNOMER, which holds the four letters; the town is in Alaska.
explanation.definitionFit: This gold-rush town lies on the Seward Peninsula of the far northern US state.

clue.text: Drew out the second I rang

parts.note: s is the standard abbreviation for second
phoned means rang on the telephone

explanation.surface: Someone recounting the moment they made a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing liquid out through a tube is the action described.

indicators.note: hold within, so the doctors surround the artists

parts.note: MOs are medical officers, doctors
RAs are Royal Academicians, artists

explanation.surface: In the town of Slough, doctors hug painters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slough' looks like the Berkshire town, but it means a bog.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a swamp or mire, a boggy bit of ground.

explanation.surface: Guiding a vehicle along a straight route.
explanation.definitionFit: To guide something is to aim it, and the adjective means straight, without deviation.

clue.text: I'm not poor anyway, but this should make me richer

indicators.note: read as 'any way', in any order, telling us to rearrange the letters

explanation.surface: A speaker insisting they are not poor but would still like a raise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' looks like a mere filler, but it signals rearranging I'M NOT POOR; 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being moved up a rank at work normally brings a pay rise and so more wealth.

parts.note: read as the central part of the eye, which the phrase 'apple of the eye' originally meant, and as a teacher's favourite student

explanation.surface: A teacher's favourite child.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'apple of the eye' first meant the eye's centre, and a teacher's charge is a schoolchild.

clue.text: Letter from abroad, from soldier's retired mother

indicators.note: something that has retired has gone back, so this piece is read backwards

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier, so GI's
ma is mother

explanation.surface: A letter posted from overseas by a soldier's mother who has stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns GIS into SIG. 'Letter from abroad' is a foreign letter of the alphabet, not a posted one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek alphabet's eighteenth character is a foreign letter.

indicators.note: the two words between them supply the letters, spanning the end of one and start of the other

explanation.surface: Summer excursions bring pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish or zest in doing something is keen enjoyment.

definitions.meaning: an archbishop holding the chief rank in a province
Tarzan was brought up by apes, which are members of the highest order of mammals

explanation.surface: A bishop playing guardian to the jungle hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Tarzan, Edgar Rice Burroughs's jungle hero, was reared by great apes.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop is the chief cleric of a province, and apes belong to the zoological order including humans.

clue.text: No tough guy, but gets money out of work

parts.note: to milk someone is to extract money from them
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A weakling who nonetheless profits from a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeble, timid man is the opposite of a hard man.

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the word sounds like the answer

parts.note: to lead is to play first, as in a card game

explanation.surface: A football team kicks off first.
explanation.walkthrough: United stands for the football club Leeds United, a Yorkshire side.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire football club bears the city's name followed by United.

parts.note: Benedick is the confirmed bachelor of Much Ado About Nothing who finally marries; a newly married man traditionally carries his bride across the doorway

explanation.surface: A question about what Shakespeare's reluctant lover has to bring across.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridegroom carries his bride across the doorstep of the new home.
